tier_reason: Independent measurement by a competing project (SampleRateTap), whose harness async/bench/compare/bench_compare.cpp (Google Benchmark) is public and whose COMPARISON.md states GCC 13.3 -O3 (CMake Release), libsamplerate 0.2.2 and the r8brain 7.5 commit pin, but the CPU is only 'shared Xeon @ 2.10 GHz' with no model, so it falls short of A. r8brain's own repo publishes no comparison against libsamplerate or any other resampler (absolute Mrops only).

corrections.workload: Streaming conversion of a float 997 Hz sine at one fixed near-unity ratio (48000 to 48000*(1+200 ppm) Hz) in 128-frame blocks, million output frames/s, median of 5 (SampleRateTap async/bench/compare/bench_compare.cpp). r8brain runs one r8b::CDSPResampler per channel, linear phase, with ReqAtten 120 dB and a 2 % transition band (plus an 8 % band row), and with the CDSPResampler16/24 preset attenuations (136.45 and 180.15 dB, 2 % band) for the higher tier; the float-to-double (de)interleave is inside the timed loop. libsamplerate runs SRC_SINC_MEDIUM_QUALITY and SRC_SINC_BEST_QUALITY via src_process. Tiers are paired by vendor-stated stopband. The same page also gives QEMU TCG instruction counts per stereo output frame on Cortex-M55, Cortex-M33 and Hexagon.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Third-party table (Mframes/s, higher is better), ~120 dB tier: r8brain ReqAtten 120 dB (default 2 % band) mono 35.4 vs libsamplerate MEDIUM 5.2 (about 6.8x, derived from page data), stereo 16.5 vs 4.8 (about 3.4x, derived), 8-ch 4.1 vs 1.9 (about 2.2x, derived); with the 8 % band, stereo 17.9 (about 3.7x, derived). ~140 dB tier, stereo: r8brain at CDSPResampler16 settings (136.45 dB) 18.4 vs libsamplerate BEST 1.6 (about 11.5x, derived), at CDSPResampler24 settings (180.15 dB) 14.1 (about 8.8x, derived). Embedded steady-state instructions per stereo output frame (lower is better), r8brain 120 dB default band vs libsamplerate MEDIUM: Cortex-M55 1,002 vs 2,203 (about 2.2x fewer, derived), Cortex-M33 30,004 vs 49,206 (about 1.6x, derived), Hexagon 6,060 vs 9,025 (about 1.5x, derived). The r8brain README itself states only an absolute rate (38*n_cores Mrops, 56*n_cores with Intel IPP, CDSPResampler24, 44100 to 96000, Ryzen 3700X) and names no baseline.
corrections.caveats: Numbers come from a competitor's comparison page (SampleRateTap), not from the r8brain project; r8brain's README publishes no comparison and asks that competing libraries be tuned to linear phase and similar stop-band. The same table shows soxr HQ/VHQ about 1.7-3.2x faster than r8brain in every row (derived from page data), so r8brain beats libsamplerate but is not the fastest resampler measured. Large latency trade-off: r8brain's FFT block convolution withholds 789 input frames (16.4 ms) at the 120 dB default band and 1,700-1,782 frames (35-37 ms) at the ~140 dB tier, against 46 frames (0.96 ms) for libsamplerate MEDIUM and 143 frames (3.0 ms) for BEST; the passband-matched 8 % band still costs 200 frames (4.2 ms). Tier pairing is by vendor-stated stopband; the CDSPResampler16-setting row (136.45 dB) has a lower stopband than libsamplerate BEST (~144 dB), while the CDSPResampler24-setting row (180.15 dB, still 8.8x) exceeds it; r8brain's 2 % transition band is narrower than libsamplerate MEDIUM's, so the 120 dB row is not doing less filtering. Only one near-unity ratio was timed; the README warns performance varies greatly with ratio. CPU model only 'shared Xeon @ 2.10 GHz'. The benchmark used r8brain 7.5 with the Ooura FFT; version 7.6 (2026-09-30) speeds up filter calculation (a one-time construction cost), which does not change the steady-state throughput measured here. On the Cortex-M builds r8brain's filter-cache std::mutex was replaced by a no-op lock. Ratios are derived from page data.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 743 stars, 84 forks; README lists users including REAPER, Audirvana, Red Dead Redemption 2 and OpenMPT

notes: All Mframes/s numbers match the r8brain and libsamplerate rows of COMPARISON.md and the harness code matches the stated settings (ReqAtten 120/136.45/180.15, fprLinearPhase, SRC_SINC_MEDIUM/BEST_QUALITY). The QEMU instruction-count table has public code, named compilers (arm-none-eabi-gcc 13.2.1, hexagon-clang 19.1.5, -O3) and named cores, but counts instructions rather than time, so I kept B. tier_reason: A single first-party README sentence ('about 25% faster than the flac reference decoder application on x86_64 systems', last changed in commit 7eb71412 on 2018-08-05) with no benchmark code, machine, compiler, flags or input files; the repo's test/ directory holds only correctness tests (test_flac_integration_runner.py compares output with the flac decoder and times nothing).

corrections.baseline: flac command-line reference decoder application (Xiph flac, built on libFLAC); no comparison against libFLAC's API, FFmpeg or dr_flac is published
corrections.caveats: Single README sentence from August 2018 (so the flac decoder of that era, likely 1.3.x), no numbers beyond '25%', no benchmark code, no machine, compiler or flags stated, and no input files named. The baseline is the flac command-line application, which also writes an output file and, as far as I know, verifies the stream MD5 by default, whereas libfoxenflac stores the STREAMINFO MD5 field but never computes it (CRC checks are on by default), so the two may not do the same work. No comparison against libFLAC's API, FFmpeg or dr_flac exists. The author says the code is not optimised and that ARM6 performance is significantly worse. Re-licensed to LGPL-2.1-or-later in March 2025. Last commit 2025-03-29 (README fix).

notes: The claim is real but thin and dated: no machine is stated, the baseline is the flac CLI rather than libFLAC itself, and nothing was published against dr_flac or FFmpeg (one WebSearch found no independent numbers). Metadata confirmed: 84 stars, LGPL-2.1-or-later, not a fork, last commit 2025-03-29, so stale.

tier_reason: First-party README tables of perf clockticks on an i7-6700K against keyj's minimp3; scripts/perf.sh (perf stat -e cycles over vectors/*.bit) is public, but the compiler and flags used for the table are not stated and the keyj harness is not published, so it stays C.

corrections.caveats: Baseline is the original keyj minimp3, a small fixed-point hobby decoder that fails conformance on every vector (PSNR 71-72 dB on most, 27.80 dB on si_huff.bit and 0.15 dB on sin1k0db.bit) and decodes nothing on he_free.bit, so on several vectors it is not producing correct output (sin1k0db sample counts also differ, 730,368 vs 725,760); the speed rows compare a conformant decoder with a broken one. No number against libmpg123, libmad, FFmpeg or dr_mp3 is published in the repo, and none was found elsewhere. The only independent figure found is FastLED's Callgrind count (agents/docs/mp3-decoder-performance.md, its vendored minimp3-float build, scalar -DMINIMP3_NO_SIMD at -O2, x86-64): 202,832,660 instructions vs 222,939,814 for the Helix MP3 decoder, about 9% fewer, instruction counts rather than time. Compiler and flags for the README table are not stated (the CI script scripts/build.sh builds with gcc -O2 -std=c89); the timed process includes file I/O and the PSNR comparison against the reference PCM. Numbers are first-party, from an i7-6700K, and the README calls it a 'rough benchmark'. CC0-1.0 dedication carries no patent grant.

notes: All four quoted clocktick pairs match the README tables. Asked about stronger baselines: none against libmpg123, FFmpeg or dr_mp3 exists (dr_mp3 is itself derived from minimp3); FastLED's Callgrind table against Helix (AMD EPYC 7763, clang 18, -O2 scalar) is the only independent number, a 9% instruction-count edge for its vendored float build, so I noted it in caveats rather than upgrading. Metadata confirmed: CC0-1.0, about 2.0k stars, 271 forks, not a fork, last commit 2026-07-27.
